answer.exemplar: In the first two cantos the traveller is presented in the third person as Childe Harold, a young Englishman abroad whose own story is kept at a distance. From the third canto the poem speaks in the first person as the poet, and the fourth becomes an essayistic meditation on Italy's ruins and vanished greatness. The change makes the later cantos confessional and historical, and it removes the protection of a created character.

questions.explanation: A third-person traveller lets the poet narrate another man's journey before he speaks as himself. Treating the later cantos as more travel writing misses the confession and the history they take on.
questions.hint: Ask who is speaking in the first two cantos.

questions.topic: Don Juan printed in a periodical and left unfinished
questions.learningObjective: Explain how instalment publication and an unfinished close shape the comic poem.
questions.stem: You want to explain to a reading group why a long poem published in instalments has no ending. Explain the arrangement and what the lack of an ending means.

answer.exemplar: The poem reached readers through a monthly magazine from 1819, so each instalment had to stand on its own while the author continued the story at his own pace. Its author died in 1824 with the work unfinished, and a further portion was published after his death. The missing close is therefore part of the poem's history, and its digressive, unfinished quality has shaped how it has been read ever since.

questions.explanation: Serial publication and the author's death are two different pressures on the same book. Explaining the poem's shape without them leaves its looseness looking careless rather than chosen.
questions.hint: Ask what the instalments had to do and what ended them.

answer.exemplar: The sonnet's octave rhymes ABBAABBA and its sestet CDCD with a closing couplet EE, so the sounds that bound the first eight lines are never taken up again. questions.explanation: The form is complete but the resolution is withheld. To explain the sonnet only as a sonnet misses what the rhyme scheme is doing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and the change of speaker in its later cantos
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what the change of speaker gains in the later cantos.
questions.stem: You weigh the change of speaker in a pilgrimage poem's later cantos. Which judgement best describes what the change gains?

options.text: The later cantos gain balance, since the change removes the need for the poem's original subject.
options.misconception: claims the change removes the subject

options.text: The later cantos gain clarity, since a third-person narrator is easier to follow than a first.
options.misconception: reverses which person is clearer

options.text: The later cantos gain nothing, since a traveller's voice was better suited to a travel poem.
options.misconception: denies the change brings any gain

options.text: The later cantos gain directness, since the poet stops hiding behind a traveller and speaks as himself.

questions.explanation: Speaking as himself makes the later cantos more exposed and more direct, which is the point of abandoning the persona. The other judgements either claim the change undoes the poem's subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader now has that the early cantos withheld.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prometheus Unbound and the kind of work its subtitle announces
questions.learningObjective: Infer what follows for a reader when the unbound drama has no stage directions.
questions.stem: You note that a work called a lyrical drama in four acts has no stage directions and no scenery. What follows for a reader?

options.text: That the text is meant to be read for its voice and argument, not staged as a performed drama.
That the work is an incomplete play whose stage directions were lost in printing.
options.misconception: calls the missing directions a printing loss

options.text: That the work was staged by a company that preferred improvisation.
options.misconception: invents an improvised staging

options.text: That the work is really a set of songs with no dramatic pretension at all.
options.misconception: denies the dramatic shape of the work

questions.explanation: A work without stage directions or scenery is a play-shaped text for the reader and the voice, as the subtitle announced. Lost directions, improvised staging and mere songs contradict the book's form.
questions.hint: Ask what a text without directions is for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Kubla Khan's preface and the incompleteness it puts on the record
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what the printed confession does to the reader's expectations.
questions.stem: You consider the effect of a preface that ends by confessing that a poem's rest is gone for ever. What does that do to the reader's expectations?

options.text: It raises the expectation of a sequel, since the lost part must exist somewhere.
options.misconception: treats the confession as a promise

options.text: It removes the expectation of completion and replaces it with attention to the surviving fragment.
It lowers the reader's trust in the poem, since the poet admits he cannot finish.
options.misconception: reads the confession as a mark of unreliability

options.text: It has no effect, since a preface is read after the poem and cannot change it.
options.misconception: denies that a preface can shape reading

questions.explanation: A confession of permanent loss withdraws the expectation of an ending. A sequel, a distrust and a claim of no effect all misjudge what the printed confession accomplishes.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader stops waiting for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ozymandias and the rhyme the octave never resolves
questions.learningObjective: Infer what a count of rhyme sounds shows about the sonnet's octave.

stimulus.body: A note counts the rhyme sounds of a sonnet: the first eight lines use two rhymes, each repeated four times; the next six introduce two new rhymes, each twice; and the closing couplet uses a fifth rhyme twice. No rhyme sound of the first eight lines appears again.

questions.stem: What does the note's count show about the sonnet's octave?

options.text: That its rhymes are repeated in the couplet, so the poem closes properly.
options.misconception: claims the couplet reuses the octave's rhyme

options.text: That the sonnet has one rhyme too many for the form it uses.
options.misconception: treats the count as a technical excess

options.text: That its rhymes are never resumed, so the first eight lines are left open rather than answered.
That the sestet's rhymes were supplied by a later editor to complete the poem.
options.misconception: invents later editorial work

questions.explanation: The note's last clause is decisive: because the octave's rhyme sounds never recur. Repeating them, exceeding the form and later editorial repair all contradict the count as given.
questions.hint: Read the note's final sentence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Lay of the Last Minstrel as a performance put inside a poem
questions.learningObjective: Explain the performance device in the border poem and what it produces.
questions.stem: Your club meeting needs a version of how a border poem is built as a song sung inside a story. Explain the device and what it produces.

answer.exemplar: The poem opens with a narrator who meets an old singer and asks him to perform, and the tale is then given as that singer's performance, closing on the song itself rather than on any comment about it. The device makes the poem an act of listening: the reader hears a voice telling someone else's story, and the singer's own voice, its roughness and its turns of phrase become part of what the story means.

questions.explanation: Putting a singer inside the poem means the story is delivered, not simply narrated. Explaining the frame without that listening relation leaves out the effect the device was built for.
questions.hint: Ask what the singer's own voice adds to the tale.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Don Juan printed in a periodical and left unfinished
questions.learningObjective: Defend the reading of the comic poem's unfinished state as a deliberate feature.
questions.stem: You must defend a claim that a comic poem printed in instalments and never finished is a deliberate artistic choice rather than a failure. What is the best defence?

options.text: No defence is possible, since the poet plainly ran out of time and material.
options.misconception: concedes that the ending is simply a failure

options.text: The defence is that no reader has ever noticed that the poem stops.
options.misconception: invents an unnoticing audience

options.text: The defence is that the poem was meant to be read only in the years of its publication.
options.misconception: limits the poem to its first audience

options.text: Its serial form and its refusal of a conclusion work with the comic subject, so the ending is a feature.

questions.explanation: The strongest defence shows form and theme working together: a comic poem about business that will not conclude enacts what it says. Conceding failure and claiming nobody noticed give up the argument.
questions.hint: Ask what a novel's title names, and what this one names.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The chained rhyme of the five sections of the Ode to the West Wind
questions.learningObjective: Explain what carries an ode forward through its chained rhymes.
questions.stem: You ask what makes an ode's chained rhymes carry a poem forward. Which statement is best?

options.text: Each group of rhymes opens into the next, so the ear is pulled onward and the movement never settles.
The chaining reduces the number of rhymes, so the poem reaches its end more quickly.
options.misconception: claims chaining speeds the poem to its end

options.text: The chaining is required by the form, since an ode must have five sections in all.
options.misconception: makes the chain a rule about section count

options.text: The chaining shows that the poem was revised from a shorter work of its own.
options.misconception: infers revision from the chaining

questions.explanation: The chaining works because each group's rhymes open into the next. Fewer rhymes, a rule about section counts and a revision from a shorter poem explain nothing about how the movement works.
questions.hint: Ask what happens at the end of each group of rhymes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The Lay of the Last Minstrel as a performance put inside a poem
questions.learningObjective: Defend the claim that the inner singer makes the story easier to bear.
questions.stem: You argue that a singer placed inside the poem makes the story's violence easier to bear. What grounds support you?

options.text: A singer inside the poem guarantees that the tale is historically accurate.
options.misconception: confuses a frame with documentary truth

options.text: A named singer tells of the cruelty in his own judgement and pace, so it reaches us as report, not scene.
A singer inside the poem makes the poem a secret, since only insiders could hear it.
options.misconception: treats the frame as secrecy

options.text: A singer inside the poem proves that the poem was a record of a real performance.
options.misconception: treats the frame as a transcript

questions.explanation: A voice telling the story places a mediating judgement between the reader. Documentary truth, secrecy and a transcript of a real performance each rest on a misreading of the frame.
questions.hint: Ask where the telling sits between the reader and the event.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border as an edited rather than a collected anthology
questions.learningObjective: Describe the editor's work from the evidence of his scholarly apparatus.

stimulus.body: A note on an eighteenth-century collection of songs records that the editor printed for each piece the manuscripts and printed books he had used, marked which verses were missing from his sources, filled some of them from other copies, and in a few cases cut a song he judged spurious.

questions.stem: From the note, which description of the editor's work is best supported?

options.text: He was a collector who printed every song he could find, with nothing left out and nothing added.
options.misconception: assumes the editor printed without selection

options.text: He was a poet who wrote all the songs himself and printed them under old names.
options.misconception: makes the collection a forgery of one author's work

options.text: He was an editor making choices, restoring and rejecting, and he let the reader see the grounds for them.
He was a printer who copied the songs exactly as they appeared in the books he used.
options.misconception: reduces the editor to a copyist

questions.explanation: Printing sources, marking gaps and cutting a song are acts of judgement made visible, so the editor's work can be checked. Forging originals contradicts that practice.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader could check.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Kubla Khan's preface and the incompleteness it puts on the record
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a preface can be read as part of the poem it introduces.
questions.stem: For a talk you set out to explain how a preface can be read as part of a poem rather than as an introduction to it. Use the case of the fragment composed in a sleep.

answer.exemplar: The preface describes a poem composed whole during a deep sleep and interrupted by a visitor, so that only part of it could be written down and the rest was lost. Read as an introduction, that is an anecdote; read as part of the work, it is the poem's account of its own origin and of the gap at its end, which is why the shortfall was printed on the title page and could not be filled in without the reader's complicity.

questions.explanation: The preface gives the only account of how the fragment came to be, so it is the poem's own testimony rather than commentary. Treating it as an introduction leaves the gap unexplained.
questions.hint: Ask what the preface knows that the verses cannot tell us.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ozymandias and the rhyme the octave never resolves
questions.learningObjective: Compare two sonnets and explain why the unresolved rhyme suits its subject.
questions.stem: A seminar group asks you to compare a sonnet whose rhymes are left hanging with one that closes its rhymes neatly. Which reading best accounts for why the first suits its subject?

options.text: The hanging rhymes are simpler to write, so the poem's plainness matches its plain subject.
options.misconception: explains the effect by ease of composition

options.text: The hanging rhymes show the poet was working to a deadline for a periodical.
options.misconception: invents a deadline to explain the form

options.text: The hanging rhymes show the poem was written for a reader who knew the original language.
options.misconception: makes the audience an explanation of the scheme

options.text: A refusal of resolution sounds like the emptiness its subject describes, so the form argues the content.

questions.explanation: The formal withholding and the subject matter reinforce one another, so the reader hears the emptiness of the poem's world in its unclosed rhymes. Ease of writing explains nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the open rhymes sound like beside the subject.
